pl-l2d24c1-d1e108.summary: Asks what grace or power man had before the fall and whether by it he could stand.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e111.summary: Answers that, as with the angels, man at creation was given a help of grace and power by which he could stand, not falling from what he had, but not advance so as to merit salvation by the grace of creation alone. By it he could resist evil but not accomplish good; live without sin, but not live spiritually so as to merit eternal life without further grace.
claims: The grace of creation enabled standing, not merit.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e114.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: man was made upright, able to remain so, not without divine help, and to become perverse by his own choice; whichever he chose, God's will would be done by him or concerning him; because he preferred his own will, God's will was done concerning him.
claims: Man could remain upright with God's help.
God's will is fulfilled either way.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e118.summary: Further Enchiridion: man had to be made able to will good and evil, not fruitlessly if good, not unpunished if evil.
claims: Man was made able to will good or evil.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e121.summary: Cites De correptione et gratia: if angel or man had lacked this help when first made, since their nature could not remain without divine help, they would not have fallen by their own fault.
claims: Without the help of grace the fall would not have been culpable.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e126.summary: Further Augustine: God gave man a good will, in which he made him upright, and a help without which he could not remain in it if he willed, and by which he could; that he would will it he left to his choice.
claims: God gave good will and the help to remain in it.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e129.summary: Further Augustine: he received the ability if he willed, but did not have the will by which he could; had he had it, he would have persevered.
claims: Adam had the power but not the will to persevere.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e132.summary: Concludes that man received rectitude, good will, and help by which he could stand at creation; otherwise he would not seem to fall by his own fault.
claims: Adam had rectitude and helping grace.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e135.summary: Asks how man had an upright and good will if he could neither merit life by it nor willed to stand by it.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e139.summary: Answers that he willed nothing evil then, and willed to stand for a time but not perseveringly, so his will then was upright and good.
claims: Adam's will was good but not persevering.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e142.summary: Objection: by the grace of creation he could stand and resist temptation; resisting evil is meritorious; so he could advance by the grace of creation without other grace.

pl-l2d24c1-d1e145.summary: Answers that resisting evil would not have been meritorious for him, since nothing in him impelled him to evil, as standing was not meritorious for the angels who did not fall. For us, not doing evil is sometimes meritorious, where a cause moves us to it, since by sin's corruption our steps are prone to fall; declining evil always avoids punishment but does not always merit the palm.
claims: Resisting evil merits only where there is inclination to evil.
Avoiding evil avoids punishment but does not always merit.

pl-l2d24c1.summary: Asks what grace or power man had before the fall and whether he could stand by it. As with the angels, man received at creation a help of grace and power by which he could stand, not falling from what he had, but not advance to merit salvation without further grace; he could resist evil but not accomplish good, live without sin but not live spiritually to merit eternal life. Augustine: man was made upright, able to remain with divine help or become perverse by his own choice; had the help been lacking, his fall would not have been his fault; 'he received the ability if he willed, but not the will to use it.' His will was upright, since he willed nothing evil and willed to stand for a time, though not perseveringly. Resisting temptation would not have been meritorious for him, since nothing within impelled him to evil, as with the angels who stood; for us resisting is meritorious only where something inclines us to evil.
claims: Man received at creation a help of grace enabling him to stand.
By creation's grace he could avoid evil but not merit eternal life.
Without that help, his fall would not have been his fault.
He had the power to stand if he willed, but not the will to persevere.
His will was upright, though not persevering.
Resisting evil was not meritorious for him, since nothing inclined him to evil.
Resisting evil merits only where something inclines us toward it.
